title: Principles Must be Proven; Use “Value Drills” to Help
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart builds on a reader's letter from educator Camille to argue that stating values, for teachers or students, is not enough; values have to be proven in action or they produce hypocrisy. Camille's idea of small value drills, such as running to the next telephone pole because you said you would, treats character as something practiced in low-stakes moments before the high-stakes ones arrive. In the classroom she names the value at stake, for example integrity at a reading check or honesty and self-reflection when handing back a test, and has students answer for it. Stuart's takeaway is that durable change comes through humdrum daily practice rather than willpower or dramatic moments. He closes by asking the reader to identify a value drill for today.
points: Affirming values without testing them risks cultivating the hypocritical life rather than the values-driven one.
Character is built by practice in small moments, not by willpower in the big one, so teachers should create low-stakes chances to act on a named value.
Concrete classroom drills include asking students to answer honestly whether they did the reading and framing a test as a chance to show honesty and self-reflection.
The same drill logic applies to teachers' own stated principles, which must also be proven daily.
quotes: First, for us and our students, there’s actually a danger in stopping at mere value affirmation. You and I can state principles like those that I start this blog article with — that’s easy. But if we end up living in contrast to those values, we’re cultivating not the values-driven life, but the hypocritical one!

And second, the path to living a value-driven life — a life where one’s principles are proven daily, where an integrated character is day-by-day solidifying — isn’t willpower, it’s practice. Camille calls these “value drills” — little points in the day where she demonstrates to herself that she is a person of integrity because she said she’d run to that next pole and then she did that no matter how she felt.

This is brilliant because this is perhaps the fundamental way that human beings change — not in the giant moments, but in the small ones; not in the championship matches at the end of the season, but in the humdrum practices after school each day.

Kids can say they have certain values (honesty, work ethic), but IF they act in ways that are not aligned with values, they don’t necessarily see the problem. Or they say, “This is not who I am.” But it is, at least at that moment. But they can change if given opportunities and practice!

How this translates in the classroom is naming the values students are able to practice. After an assigned reading, for example, I can say to my class, “This is an opportunity for you to demonstrate your integrity and honesty: did you do the reading?” I say this once and expect every student to make eye contact with me and say yes or no. I thank them for their honesty, and I praise those who showed responsibility.

Another way: when passing out a test, I say, “This is an opportunity for you to demonstrate your honesty and self-reflection. If you did not prepare well, you can still be a person with integrity and honesty. And afterwards you can reflect, another good skill, and then study harder/better the next time.
